title: TCS Partners With Anthropic to Build Enterprise AI Unit, Arms 50,000 Staff With Claude
excerpt: India's largest IT services firm creates a dedicated business unit for Anthropic's Claude models, targeting regulated sectors from finance to healthcare.
body:
Tata Consultancy Services has signed a global strategic partnership with Anthropic, the frontier AI company behind Claude, to scale enterprise AI adoption across regulated industries. The deal, announced on June 11, makes TCS a Global Premier Partner in the Claude Partner Network and will see the company establish a dedicated business unit focused on deploying Anthropic's models.

Under the agreement, TCS will equip 50,000 associates across engineering, finance, legal, marketing, and sales functions with enterprise-wide access to Claude. The company says first-hand internal deployment will generate insights it can then apply to client engagements — a strategy of eating its own cooking before serving customers.

Bridging the AI Pilot Gap

The partnership is aimed squarely at a persistent problem in enterprise AI: the gap between experimentation and production. In regulated industries — financial services, healthcare, life sciences, aviation, and public services — most AI initiatives never get past the pilot stage, stalled by requirements around accuracy, auditability, and regulatory compliance.

TCS and Anthropic will jointly go to market with AI solutions across these sectors, combining TCS's consulting and implementation expertise with Anthropic's model capabilities. The companies plan to co-innovate solutions for domain-specific workflows, software modernization, and customer experience transformation.

TCS will also contribute to Anthropic's Claude Code ecosystem, building reusable skills and plugins for specialized use cases like claims adjudication and lending advisory — areas where domain knowledge is as important as the underlying AI.

"This collaboration will help customers move faster to production, particularly in industries where trust, resilience, and regulatory discipline are critical."

— K Krithivasan, CEO and Managing Director, TCS

Anthropic's India Push

For Anthropic, the TCS deal deepens its commitment to India, which the company has described as its second-largest market globally. Over the past year, the San Francisco-based startup has opened an office in India, hired for leadership positions, and expanded ties with major IT services firms.

The deal follows a similar playbook to Anthropic's partnership with rival Infosys, struck in February. OpenAI has also moved into the space, enlisting both Infosys and HCLTech as enterprise distribution partners. The race among frontier AI companies to lock in enterprise channels through India's IT services giants has become a defining trend of 2026.

Beyond Consulting: Products and Platforms

The partnership extends beyond consulting engagements into TCS's own products and platforms. Diligenta, TCS's FCA-regulated life and pensions business in the United Kingdom serving over 22 million customers, will deploy Claude for customer service and agentic process automation at scale.

TCS iON, the company's digital learning platform that conducts more than 75 million assessments annually across India, will introduce training and certification programs focused on Anthropic's models — a move that could significantly expand the talent pool for Claude-based development.

The AI Anxiety in Indian IT

The partnership arrives against a backdrop of deep investor anxiety about the future of India's $315 billion IT services sector. In February, Indian IT firms lost more than $62.8 billion in market capitalization, partly triggered by Anthropic's launch of an AI agent tool that raised fears about automation replacing traditional labour-intensive services.

"OpenAI has also moved into the space, enlisting both Infosys and HCLTech as enterprise distribution partners."

Shares of TCS and Infosys have fallen roughly 34% and 31% respectively so far in 2026. TCS Chairman N Chandrasekaran said at the company's annual general meeting that TCS expects to slow down hiring as it moves toward having an equal number of employees and AI agents in its workforce. The company cut more than 12,000 jobs last July, while headcount fell by over 23,000 on a net basis in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

For Indian IT professionals — including thousands in the diaspora working at TCS offices across the United States, United Kingdom, and Europe — the partnership underscores a fundamental shift. The same AI tools that threaten traditional services revenue are being repositioned as new growth engines. Whether that transformation generates enough value to offset the disruption remains the sector's central question.

What to Watch

The success of the partnership will hinge on whether TCS can move enterprise clients from AI pilots to production deployments at scale. With dedicated business units, early model access, and internal deployment already underway, TCS has the infrastructure in place. The question is whether regulated industries will adopt AI fast enough to justify the bet — and whether TCS can maintain margins as it trades labour arbitrage for AI-enabled services.
